identification.summary: Iran-linked cyber espionage group first publicly exposed by ClearSky and Minerva Labs in November 2015 for attacks on Israeli targets, including diplomats at Israel's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Israeli academics who study the Middle East [S1][S2]. ClearSky and Trend Micro's July 2017 'Operation Wilted Tulip' report described a broad espionage apparatus targeting government, defense and academic organizations in Israel, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the United States, Jordan and Germany [S4][S5]. Researchers describe the group as persistent and successful at exfiltrating data but lacking technical sophistication and operational discipline [S6][S8].
identification.firstObserved: ClearSky/Minerva (2015): attacks on Israeli targets since at least August 2014 [S1]. ClearSky/Trend Micro (2017): active since at least 2013 [S4][S5].
identification.notes: No Microsoft threat-actor name was found mapped to CopyKittens in the searches run; the actor record's msName is empty. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the group as CopyKittens (G0052) [S10]. The Hacker News and Security Affairs coverage of Wilted Tulip call the group 'also known as Rocket Kittens' [S5][S7], while VOA reporting distinguishes CopyKittens from the separate Iran-based group Rocket Kitten; this alias is not adopted here (see gaps). The existing alias 'Slayer Kitten' (CrowdStrike) could not be confirmed in a cited source.

attribution.sponsor: Iran (suspected). The CFR Cyber Operations Tracker lists Iran as the suspected state sponsor [S9]; ClearSky labels CopyKittens an 'Iranian threat agent' [S3].
attribution.confidence: Vendor assessment only. ClearSky and Minerva Labs estimated in 2015 that the group is a state actor or endorsed by one, based on targets, delivery methods and malware [S1]. No government attribution to CopyKittens was found; Germany's BSI described the Jerusalem Post manipulation tied to Bundestag targeting without naming a group, and the link to CopyKittens is ClearSky's assessment [S3].
attribution.basis: Targeting pattern (Israel, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, US and others hostile to Iranian interests) and malware analysis by ClearSky, Minerva Labs and Trend Micro [S1][S4][S5]; tracker listing by CFR [S9].

objectives: Long-running espionage and data theft against government ministries (including foreign affairs), defense companies, large IT companies and academic institutions in states that are regional adversaries of Iran or their partners [S1][S4][S5]. Researchers note the group exfiltrated large volumes of data despite inferior tools [S8].

sectors: Academic institutions and Middle East researchers [S1][S4]
News media websites used as watering holes [S3]
Legislators (German Bundestag offices, per ClearSky's assessment) [S3]
targeting.notes: Israeli targets dominate the early reporting [S1][S3]; the 2017 Wilted Tulip report widened the observed victim set to multiple countries [S4][S5]. Compromised Israeli news and other websites served as watering holes rather than end targets [S3].

capabilities.summary: Delivery via spear-phishing emails with weaponized documents or links, watering-hole attacks that insert a single line of JavaScript into existing libraries on compromised sites, and fake Facebook profiles used to build trust and spread malicious links [S1][S3][S4]. Malicious Office documents exploiting CVE-2017-0199 were reported in 2017 [S6]. The group also exploited web servers using SQL injection tools [S8]. Tooling includes the Matryoshka RAT (v1 from 2015, v2 in 2017), a multi-stage framework assembled from public code snippets that uses DNS for command and control and exfiltration [S1][S4]; TDTESS backdoor, Vminst lateral-movement tool, NetSrv Cobalt Strike loader and ZPP compression utility [S4][S5]; and frequent use of trial versions of Cobalt Strike, plus Metasploit and other commercially available tools [S4][S6]. MITRE lists Cobalt Strike, TDTESS, Matryoshka and Empire as associated software [S10].

campaigns.name: Early attacks on Israeli targets
campaigns.summary: ClearSky and Minerva Labs date CopyKittens attacks on Israeli targets to at least August 2014; victims included senior MFA diplomats and Israeli Middle East scholars, reached with spear-phishing documents delivering Matryoshka.

campaigns.name: First public exposure (ClearSky/Minerva report)
campaigns.summary: Joint report names the group CopyKittens and its Matryoshka malware; the vendors assess a state actor or state-endorsed group.

campaigns.name: Jerusalem Post and Israeli website watering holes (Oct 2016 - Jan 2017)
campaigns.summary: ClearSky reports the Jerusalem Post, multiple other Israeli sites and one Palestinian Authority site were compromised with injected JavaScript; ClearSky assesses with high certainty this is the incident Germany's BSI linked to targeting of the Bundestag, though BSI did not name a group.

campaigns.name: Operation Wilted Tulip
campaigns.summary: ClearSky and Trend Micro expose a wide espionage apparatus spanning the group's activity since 2013, including previously unreported tools (TDTESS, Vminst, NetSrv, ZPP), Matryoshka v2, Cobalt Strike use, and victims in six countries.

diamond.adversary: Iran-linked espionage group CopyKittens; assessed by vendors as a state or state-endorsed actor; described as persistent but noisy and lacking operational discipline [S1][S6][S8][S9].
diamond.capability: Matryoshka RAT v1/v2 with DNS C2, TDTESS backdoor, Vminst, NetSrv, ZPP, trial Cobalt Strike, Metasploit, CVE-2017-0199 documents, SQL injection tools [S1][S4][S5][S6][S8].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised legitimate news and government-adjacent websites serving injected JavaScript from actor-controlled domains; fake Facebook profiles; DNS-based C2 channels [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.victim: Foreign ministries, defense firms, IT companies, academics, legislators and UN employees in Israel, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the US, Jordan and Germany [S1][S3][S4][S5][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection against Israel and states contrary to Iranian interests, consistent with suspected Iranian state sponsorship [S1][S4][S9].
diamond.technology: Trust in frequently visited news websites, Microsoft Office document handling (CVE-2017-0199), vulnerable web applications (SQL injection) and DNS egress [S1][S3][S6][S8].

gaps: No public reporting of new CopyKittens campaigns after 2017 was found; whether the cluster remains active, was renamed, or was absorbed into another vendor cluster is unknown.
No Microsoft threat-actor name mapped to CopyKittens was found; Microsoft's naming table could not be checked directly.

Alias conflict: The Hacker News and Security Affairs say 'aka Rocket Kittens' [S5][S7], but VOA reporting says CopyKittens is distinct from Rocket Kitten; the VOA article could not be opened to cite, so the overlap is unresolved and Rocket Kitten facts must not be merged here.
The 'Slayer Kitten' (CrowdStrike) alias in the imported record was not confirmed by any source found; CrowdStrike's adversary page was not reached.
No government attribution: Germany's BSI did not name a group for the Jerusalem Post/Bundestag incident; the CopyKittens link is ClearSky's assessment [S3].

Primary PDFs (Minerva/ClearSky 2015 CopyKittens.pdf, ClearSky/Trend Micro Operation_Wilted_Tulip.pdf) and vendor pages could not be fetched; content is drawn from search-result summaries and secondary coverage.

The DomainTools 'Hunting Campaign Indicators on Privacy Protected Attack Infrastructure' case study (2017-03-21) is in the imported references, but the search result summary did not confirm it names CopyKittens; not cited.
Organizational identity (MOIS vs. IRGC vs. contractor) is not established in any source found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain includes commonly visited regional news sites and partner-government web properties that can be turned into watering holes, plus email and social media channels used to reach foreign-affairs, defense and academic staff [S1][S3][S4]. STEP 2 (effects): Watering holes on trusted media sites can reach legislators and staff of partner nations (e.g., Bundestag offices per ClearSky) without direct targeting [S3]. STEP 3 (threat evaluation): Template is spear-phish or watering hole, then Matryoshka/TDTESS or Cobalt Strike implant, lateral movement with Vminst, compression with ZPP, and DNS or HTTP exfiltration; tradecraft is noisy and reuses commodity tooling [S1][S4][S5][S6]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is persistent collection against Israeli, Gulf, Turkish, US and German government, defense and academic targets for policy intelligence [S4][S5]. MDCOA is a watering-hole compromise of a regional news or partner-government site frequented by coalition personnel to gain footholds in DoD-adjacent or partner networks [S3]. Candidate indicators: unexpected single-line JavaScript additions to site libraries, Office documents exploiting CVE-2017-0199, anomalous DNS query volumes or encoded subdomains, and Cobalt Strike trial-version artifacts [S1][S3][S4][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: this cluster's latest public reporting is 2017; treat it as a historical case and correlate with current Iranian clusters before tasking [S4]. (2) Authorities: attribution rests on vendor assessments, not government statements, so products should label confidence accordingly [S1][S3]. (3) Mission assurance: DNS egress monitoring and Office patching address the documented C2 and delivery paths [S1][S6]. (4) Coordination: watering holes on partner-nation media and legislative targeting (Germany) argue for sharing indicators with partner CERTs such as BSI and Israeli counterparts [S3].
